lessons.title: Speed, Velocity, and Acceleration
lessons.content: Speed tells us how fast something is moving — it equals distance divided by time (speed = distance/time). If you walk 10 km in 2 hours, your speed is 5 km/h. Velocity is speed with a direction: 5 km/h north. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity — how quickly something speeds up or slows down. Acceleration = change in velocity / time. If a car goes from 0 to 60 km/h in 10 seconds, its acceleration is 6 km/h per second. Deceleration (negative acceleration) means slowing down.
examples: A cheetah runs 100m in 4s: speed = 100/4 = 25 m/s
A car accelerates from 0 to 20 m/s in 5s: acceleration = 20/5 = 4 m/s²
A ball thrown up decelerates at 9.8 m/s² due to gravity

keyTerms.speed: Distance traveled per unit of time
keyTerms.acceleration: Rate of change of velocity over time

quiz.question: A cyclist travels 30 km in 2 hours. What is the speed?
quiz.explanation: Speed = distance/time = 30/2 = 15 km/h

quiz.question: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
quiz.explanation: Velocity is speed with a direction specified.

quiz.question: A car goes from 0 to 30 m/s in 6 seconds. Acceleration?
quiz.explanation: a = change in velocity / time = 30/6 = 5 m/s²

quiz.question: A runner completes 400m in 50s. Average speed?
Deceleration means:
quiz.explanation: Deceleration is negative acceleration — velocity is decreasing.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
lessons.content: Isaac Newton described three laws governing motion. First Law (Inertia): An object stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line unless a force acts on it. Second Law: Force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma). A heavier object needs more force to accelerate. Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When you push a wall, the wall pushes back with equal force.
examples: First Law: Passengers lurch forward when a bus stops — their body wants to keep moving
Second Law: Pushing a 20 kg cart with 40 N gives acceleration of 2 m/s²
Third Law: A rocket pushes exhaust down, the gas pushes the rocket up

keyTerms.inertia: The tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion
keyTerms.force: A push or pull measured in Newtons (N)
keyTerms.Newton: The SI unit of force; 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²
keyTerms.resultant force: The overall net force on an object when all forces are combined

quiz.question: What force accelerates a 5 kg object at 3 m/s²?
Newton's First Law is also called:
quiz.explanation: The First Law describes inertia — objects resist changes in motion.

quiz.question: When you walk, the ground pushes you:
quiz.explanation: Third Law: equal and opposite reaction pushes you forward.

quiz.question: A 10 kg object with resultant force 50 N has acceleration:
An object at constant velocity has resultant force of:
quiz.explanation: Constant velocity = no acceleration = zero resultant force (First Law).

lessons.title: Gravity and Weight
lessons.content: Gravity is an attractive force between any two objects with mass. On Earth, gravity pulls everything toward the center with an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s². Weight is the force of gravity on an object: Weight = mass × g (W = mg). Mass is the amount of matter (kg) and stays the same everywhere. Weight changes depending on gravity — you'd weigh less on the Moon (g = 1.6 m/s²) but your mass stays the same.
examples: A 60 kg person on Earth: weight = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N
Same person on Moon: weight = 60 × 1.6 = 96 N (but still 60 kg mass)
A dropped ball accelerates at 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance)

keyTerms.gravity: The force of attraction between objects with mass
keyTerms.weight: The force of gravity acting on an object's mass (W = mg)
keyTerms.mass: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms
keyTerms.gravitational field strength: The force per unit mass due to gravity (g ≈ 9.8 N/kg on Earth)

quiz.question: Weight of a 10 kg object on Earth? (g = 10 m/s²)
On the Moon, your mass would:
quiz.explanation: Mass doesn't change with location.

quiz.question: Two objects dropped from same height (no air resistance) — which lands first?
options: They hit at the same time
quiz.explanation: Gravity accelerates all objects equally at 9.8 m/s².

quiz.question: Weight is measured in:
quiz.explanation: Weight is a force, so it's measured in Newtons.

quiz.question: An astronaut floats in space because:
options: There is no gravity in space
They are in freefall — gravity still acts but they fall with the spacecraft
quiz.explanation: Astronauts are in continuous freefall — gravity is still present, they just fall together with the station.

lessons.title: Friction and Air Resistance
lessons.content: Friction is a force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact. It acts in the opposite direction to movement. Friction depends on: the roughness of surfaces (rough = more friction) and the force pressing surfaces together (heavier = more friction). Friction can be useful (grip on shoes, brakes) or problematic (wear on machines, wasted energy). Air resistance (drag) is friction with air — it increases with speed and surface area. Terminal velocity occurs when air resistance equals weight — the object stops accelerating and falls at constant speed. Parachutes work by increasing air resistance.
examples: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity (~55 m/s) when air resistance balances their weight
Ice is slippery because there's very little friction between the ice and your shoe
Lubricants (oil, grease) reduce friction between machine parts, reducing wear and heat

keyTerms.friction: A force opposing motion between two surfaces in contact
keyTerms.air resistance: The friction force acting on objects moving through air (drag)
keyTerms.terminal velocity: The constant speed when air resistance equals weight — no more acceleration
keyTerms.lubrication: Using oil or grease to reduce friction between surfaces

quiz.question: Friction acts in which direction?
options: Opposite to the direction of motion
quiz.explanation: Friction always opposes (resists) the direction of movement.

quiz.question: At terminal velocity:
options: Air resistance equals weight — no acceleration
quiz.explanation: Forces are balanced (drag = weight), so velocity is constant.

quiz.question: A parachute works by:
options: Increasing air resistance to slow the fall
quiz.explanation: The large surface area increases drag, reducing terminal velocity to a safe speed.

quiz.question: More friction is useful for:
quiz.explanation: Brakes and shoe soles need friction to grip — without it, you'd slide.

quiz.question: What reduces friction between machine parts?
quiz.explanation: Lubricants create a thin film between surfaces, reducing contact and friction.

lessons.title: Pressure
lessons.content: Pressure is force spread over an area: Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A), measured in Pascals (Pa) or N/m². The same force creates more pressure on a smaller area — that's why knife blades are sharp (small area = high pressure to cut) and snowshoes are wide (large area = low pressure to avoid sinking). In fluids (liquids and gases), pressure acts in all directions. Liquid pressure increases with depth: P = ρgh (density × gravitational field strength × height). Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of air above us — about 101,325 Pa at sea level. Hydraulic systems use liquid pressure to multiply force.
examples: A 600 N person standing on both feet (area 0.04 m²): P = 600/0.04 = 15,000 Pa
Standing on one foot doubles the pressure (half the area)
Hydraulic car jack: small piston pushes with small force, large piston lifts the car with large force

keyTerms.pressure: Force per unit area: P = F/A, measured in Pascals (Pa)
keyTerms.Pascal: The SI unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m²
keyTerms.atmospheric pressure: The pressure exerted by the weight of the atmosphere (~101,325 Pa at sea level)
keyTerms.hydraulics: Using liquid pressure to transmit and multiply force

quiz.question: Pressure equals:
quiz.explanation: P = F/A. More force or less area = more pressure.

quiz.question: Why are knife blades thin?
options: Small area creates high pressure to cut easily
quiz.explanation: A thin edge concentrates force on a tiny area, creating very high pressure.

quiz.question: Liquid pressure increases with:
quiz.explanation: Deeper = more liquid above = more weight pressing down = higher pressure.

quiz.question: A 500 N force on 0.1 m² gives pressure of:
Hydraulic systems work because:
options: Pressure in a liquid is transmitted equally in all directions
quiz.explanation: Liquids are incompressible — pressure applied at one point transmits equally throughout.

lessons.title: Forms of Energy and Conservation
lessons.content: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. Forms: kinetic (motion), potential (stored — gravitational, elastic, chemical), thermal (heat), electrical, light, sound, and nuclear. The Law of Conservation of Energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transformed. When you drop a ball, potential converts to kinetic. Total energy in a closed system always stays the same.
examples: Roller coaster at top: max potential energy; at bottom: max kinetic energy
Battery: chemical energy → electrical energy
Rubbing hands: kinetic energy → thermal energy

keyTerms.potential energy: Stored energy due to position; gravitational PE = mgh
keyTerms.conservation of energy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed
keyTerms.energy transfer: Energy moving from one store to another or one form to another

quiz.question: A ball at the top of a hill has maximum:
quiz.explanation: At the top, maximum height = maximum gravitational potential energy.

quiz.question: Conservation of energy means:
options: Energy can only change form, not be created or destroyed
quiz.explanation: Total energy in a closed system remains constant — it only transforms.

quiz.question: What energy transformation occurs in a solar panel?
quiz.explanation: Solar panels convert light energy into electrical energy.

quiz.question: KE = ½mv². A 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s has KE of:
GPE = mgh. A 5 kg object at height 4m (g=10):

lessons.title: Work and Power
lessons.content: In physics, work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force. Work = Force × distance (W = Fd), measured in Joules (J). No work is done if the object doesn't move, or if force is perpendicular to movement. Power is the rate of doing work — how fast energy is transferred. Power = Work / time (P = W/t), measured in Watts (W). 1 Watt = 1 Joule per second. A more powerful engine does the same work in less time.
examples: Lifting a 10 kg box 2m high: Work = mgh = 10 × 10 × 2 = 200 J
200 J of work in 4 seconds: Power = 200/4 = 50 W
Carrying a book horizontally does zero physics work — force (up) is perpendicular to motion (forward)

keyTerms.work: Force applied over a distance in the direction of force; W = Fd
keyTerms.power: The rate of doing work; P = W/t, measured in Watts
keyTerms.joule: The SI unit of energy and work; 1 J = 1 N·m
keyTerms.watt: The SI unit of power; 1 W = 1 J/s

quiz.question: Work done pushing a box with 20 N over 5 meters?
Power if 300 J of work is done in 10 seconds?
Holding a heavy bag while standing still does how much work?
quiz.explanation: No movement = no distance = no work done.

quiz.question: A 100 W bulb uses 100 J of energy every:
quiz.explanation: 100 W = 100 J/s. So 100 J every second.

quiz.question: Two people lift the same box. Person A takes 5s, Person B takes 10s. Who is more powerful?
options: Person A — same work in less time
quiz.explanation: Same work but less time = more power. P = W/t.

lessons.title: Heat and Temperature
lessons.content: Temperature measures how hot or cold something is — it reflects the average kinetic energy of particles. Heat is the transfer of thermal energy from hotter to cooler objects. Three transfer methods: conduction (direct contact — metal spoon in hot soup), convection (fluid movement — hot air rises), and radiation (electromagnetic waves — the Sun warms Earth across space). Insulators like wood slow heat transfer; conductors like metal allow it easily.
examples: Conduction: touching a hot pan burns your hand
Convection: hot water rises, cool water sinks, creating circulation
Radiation: feeling warmth from a campfire without touching it

keyTerms.convection: Heat transfer through movement of fluids
keyTerms.radiation: Heat transfer through electromagnetic waves, no medium needed
keyTerms.insulator: A material that resists heat transfer (wood, plastic, air)

quiz.question: How does heat from the Sun reach Earth?
quiz.explanation: Space is a vacuum — only radiation can travel through it.

quiz.question: Why do metal spoons get hot in soup but wooden ones don't?
quiz.explanation: Metal conducts heat easily; wood is an insulator.

quiz.question: In convection, hot fluid:
quiz.explanation: Hot fluid is less dense and rises; cool fluid sinks.

quiz.question: Double glazed windows reduce heat loss by:
options: Trapping air (an insulator) between two panes
quiz.explanation: The trapped air layer is a poor conductor, reducing conduction and convection.

quiz.question: A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot by:
options: Eliminating conduction, convection, AND radiation transfer
quiz.explanation: Vacuum (no conduction/convection), reflective coating (minimal radiation) — all three mechanisms addressed.

lessons.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
lessons.content: No energy transfer is 100% efficient — some energy is always wasted (usually as heat). Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input × 100%. A car engine is about 25% efficient (75% wasted as heat). An LED bulb is about 90% efficient. Improving efficiency means less wasted energy and lower costs. Energy resources: non-renewable (fossil fuels, nuclear) will run out; renewable (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, tidal, biomass) are replenished naturally. The world must shift to renewables to combat climate change and resource depletion.
examples: A 100 J input bulb producing 15 J of light: efficiency = 15/100 × 100 = 15%
A car: 100 J fuel → 25 J motion + 75 J heat, sound, friction losses
Solar panels: ~20% efficient but improving — and the 'fuel' (sunlight) is free and unlimited

keyTerms.efficiency: The percentage of input energy that is usefully transferred
keyTerms.renewable energy: Energy from sources that are naturally replenished (solar, wind, hydro)
keyTerms.non-renewable energy: Energy from finite sources that will eventually run out (fossil fuels)
keyTerms.wasted energy: Energy transferred to unwanted stores, usually heat

quiz.question: A machine uses 200 J and does 50 J of useful work. Efficiency?
Most wasted energy ends up as:
quiz.explanation: Heat is the most common waste product in energy transfers.

quiz.question: Which is renewable?
quiz.explanation: Solar is renewable — the Sun provides energy without running out.

quiz.question: Why can no machine be 100% efficient?
options: Some energy is always wasted as heat due to friction
quiz.explanation: Friction and other losses mean some input energy is always wasted.

quiz.question: An LED is more efficient than a filament bulb because:
options: More energy goes to light, less to heat
quiz.explanation: LEDs convert ~90% of energy to light vs ~5% for filament bulbs.

lessons.title: Specific Heat Capacity
lessons.content: Different materials heat up at different rates. Specific heat capacity (SHC) is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Water has a high SHC (4,200 J/kg°C) — it takes a lot of energy to heat and cools slowly (that's why coastal areas have milder climates). Metals have low SHC — they heat up quickly. The equation: Energy = mass × SHC × temperature change (E = mcΔT). This calculation is used in heating systems, cooking, climate science, and engineering.
examples: Heating 2 kg of water by 5°C: E = 2 × 4200 × 5 = 42,000 J = 42 kJ
Heating 2 kg of aluminium (SHC 900) by 5°C: E = 2 × 900 × 5 = 9,000 J — much less than water
A hot water bottle stays warm for hours because water stores lots of thermal energy

keyTerms.specific heat capacity: Energy needed to raise temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C
keyTerms.thermal energy: The total kinetic energy of all particles in a substance
keyTerms.temperature change: The difference between final and initial temperature (ΔT)

quiz.question: Energy to heat 3 kg of water (SHC 4200) by 10°C?
Water has a high SHC. This means:
options: It boils at a lower temperature
It takes a lot of energy to heat up and cools slowly
quiz.explanation: High SHC = lots of energy per degree = slow to heat, slow to cool.

quiz.question: Why do coastal areas have milder climates?
options: Water's high SHC moderates temperature changes
quiz.explanation: The ocean absorbs and releases heat slowly, moderating nearby land temperatures.

quiz.question: Which heats up faster: water (SHC 4200) or iron (SHC 450)?
options: Iron — lower SHC means less energy needed per degree
quiz.explanation: Lower SHC = less energy needed = heats up faster with the same energy input.

quiz.question: E = mcΔT. If E = 8400 J, m = 2 kg, c = 4200, what is ΔT?

lessons.title: Properties of Waves
lessons.content: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy without transferring matter. Transverse waves vibrate perpendicular to travel direction (light, water ripples). Longitudinal waves vibrate parallel (sound). Every wave has: amplitude (height — energy/loudness), wavelength (distance between crests), frequency (waves per second, Hz), and speed. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = fλ).
examples: Guitar string at 440 Hz: frequency = 440 Hz (the note A)
Ocean wave: wavelength 10m, frequency 0.5 Hz: speed = 0.5 × 10 = 5 m/s
Light is transverse; sound is longitudinal

keyTerms.amplitude: Maximum displacement from rest; relates to energy
keyTerms.frequency: Waves per second, measured in Hertz (Hz)
keyTerms.transverse wave: Vibrations perpendicular to wave direction (light, water)

quiz.question: Wave with frequency 10 Hz, wavelength 3 m. Speed?
Sound is what type of wave?
quiz.explanation: Sound waves are longitudinal — particles vibrate parallel to wave direction.

quiz.question: Increasing amplitude makes sound:
quiz.explanation: Amplitude = loudness. Frequency = pitch.

quiz.question: If frequency doubles and wavelength stays the same, speed:
quiz.explanation: v = fλ. Double f with same λ = double v.

quiz.question: Wavelength is measured from:
options: Crest to crest (or compression to compression)
quiz.explanation: One complete wavelength = the distance between two consecutive identical points (crest to crest).

lessons.title: Sound
lessons.content: Sound is produced by vibrations and travels as longitudinal waves through a medium. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. It travels fastest through solids (~5000 m/s in steel), slower in liquids (~1500 m/s in water), slowest in gases (~343 m/s in air). Pitch is determined by frequency — high frequency = high pitch. Volume is determined by amplitude. Human hearing: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound (>20 kHz) is used in medical imaging and sonar.
examples: Thunder after lightning: sound (343 m/s) is much slower than light (300,000,000 m/s)
Dog whistles: above 20 kHz — too high for humans
Speaking into a cup-and-string phone: vibrations travel through the string

keyTerms.pitch: How high or low a sound is, determined by frequency
keyTerms.echo: A reflected sound wave heard after a delay
keyTerms.ultrasound: Sound above 20,000 Hz, beyond human hearing
keyTerms.vacuum: A space with no matter — sound cannot travel through it

quiz.question: Why can't sound travel in space?
quiz.explanation: Sound needs particles — space is a vacuum with none.

quiz.question: Sound travels fastest through:
quiz.explanation: Closer particles in solids transmit vibrations fastest.

quiz.question: Higher frequency = :
quiz.explanation: Frequency determines pitch. Amplitude determines loudness.

quiz.question: Ultrasound is used in:
quiz.explanation: Ultrasound waves bounce off internal structures to create images (e.g., pregnancy scans).

quiz.question: An echo is caused by:
quiz.explanation: Sound bounces off hard surfaces and returns to your ear as an echo.

lessons.title: Light and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.content: Light is an electromagnetic wave traveling at 300,000,000 m/s without needing a medium. The EM spectrum (longest to shortest wavelength): radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. Visible light: red (longest) to violet (shortest). Reflection: light bouncing off a surface (angle of incidence = angle of reflection). Refraction: light bending when passing between media (air into water).
examples: A prism splits white light into a rainbow — refraction
Mirror: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Microwaves heat food by vibrating water molecules

keyTerms.electromagnetic spectrum: Full range of EM waves from radio to gamma rays
keyTerms.visible light: The small range of EM waves humans can see (red to violet)

quiz.question: Which has the longest wavelength?
quiz.explanation: Radio waves have the longest wavelength in the EM spectrum.

quiz.question: What causes a straw to look bent in water?
quiz.explanation: Light refracts (bends) passing from water to air.

quiz.question: Speed of light is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Light travels at ~3 × 10⁸ m/s.

quiz.question: Which EM wave is used in hospital X-ray machines?
quiz.explanation: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone — creating skeleton images.

quiz.question: White light is actually:
options: A mixture of all colors of visible light
quiz.explanation: A prism proves white light is a mixture — it splits into the full visible spectrum.

lessons.title: Reflection and Mirrors
lessons.content: The law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal — an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface). In a plane (flat) mirror, the image is: the same size as the object, the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, laterally inverted (left-right swapped), and virtual (can't be projected on a screen). Concave mirrors (curved inward) can focus light — used in torches, satellite dishes, and telescopes. Convex mirrors (curved outward) give a wider field of view — used in car side mirrors and shop security mirrors.
examples: Looking in a bathroom mirror: raise your right hand, the image raises its left — lateral inversion
Torch: a concave mirror behind the bulb focuses light into a beam
Car side mirror (convex): 'objects in mirror are closer than they appear' — wider view but smaller image

keyTerms.angle of incidence: The angle between incoming light and the normal to the surface
keyTerms.normal: An imaginary line perpendicular to a surface at the point of incidence
keyTerms.virtual image: An image that cannot be projected on a screen — formed by diverging rays appearing to meet
keyTerms.lateral inversion: Left-right reversal in a mirror image

quiz.question: The angle of incidence equals:
quiz.explanation: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

quiz.question: A plane mirror image is:
quiz.explanation: Plane mirrors produce virtual, same-size, laterally inverted images.

quiz.question: Convex mirrors are used in shops because:
options: They give a wider field of view
quiz.explanation: Convex mirrors curve outward, reflecting a wider area for security monitoring.

quiz.question: The normal line is:
options: Perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence
quiz.explanation: The normal is the reference line — angles are measured from it, not from the surface.

quiz.question: Concave mirrors can:
options: Focus parallel rays to a point
quiz.explanation: Concave mirrors converge light — used in torches, telescopes, and satellite dishes.

lessons.title: Lenses and Refraction
lessons.content: Refraction occurs because light changes speed when entering a different medium. Moving from a less dense to more dense medium (air to glass), light slows down and bends toward the normal. Moving from dense to less dense (glass to air), it speeds up and bends away from the normal. Convex lenses (thicker in the middle) converge light — used in magnifying glasses, cameras, and the human eye. Concave lenses (thinner in the middle) diverge light — used to correct short-sightedness. The focal length is the distance from the lens to where parallel rays converge. Total internal reflection occurs when light hits a boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle — it reflects back instead of refracting out. This is how optical fibers work.
examples: A magnifying glass (convex lens) focuses sunlight to a point — enough to start a fire
Short-sighted people use concave lenses: the lens diverges light so it focuses correctly on the retina
Optical fibers: light bounces along inside the glass fiber by total internal reflection — used in internet cables

keyTerms.convex lens: A lens thicker in the middle that converges (focuses) light rays
keyTerms.concave lens: A lens thinner in the middle that diverges (spreads) light rays
keyTerms.focal length: The distance from a lens to the point where parallel rays converge
keyTerms.total internal reflection: Light reflecting entirely inside a medium when hitting the boundary above the critical angle

quiz.question: Light entering glass from air will:
options: Slow down and bend toward the normal
quiz.explanation: Glass is denser — light slows and bends toward the normal.

quiz.question: A magnifying glass uses a:
quiz.explanation: Convex lenses converge light and can magnify objects.

quiz.question: Optical fibers use:
quiz.explanation: Light bounces along inside the fiber by total internal reflection.

quiz.question: Short-sightedness is corrected with:
quiz.explanation: Short-sighted eyes focus before the retina — concave lenses diverge light to fix this.

quiz.question: When light goes from water to air, it bends:
quiz.explanation: Less dense medium = light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

lessons.title: Electric Circuits
lessons.content: An electric circuit is a complete path for current to flow. Current is the flow of charge (electrons), measured in Amperes (A). Voltage is the push driving current, measured in Volts (V). Resistance opposes current, measured in Ohms (Ω). Ohm's Law: V = IR. Series circuit: one path — if one component breaks, all stop. Parallel circuit: multiple branches — each operates independently.
examples: 12V battery, 4Ω resistor: I = V/R = 12/4 = 3A
Series Christmas lights: one breaks, all go out
House wiring is parallel: one light off doesn't affect others

keyTerms.current: Flow of electric charge, measured in Amperes
keyTerms.voltage: Electrical potential difference, measured in Volts
keyTerms.resistance: Opposition to current flow, measured in Ohms (Ω)
keyTerms.Ohm\u0027s Law: V = IR — voltage equals current times resistance

quiz.question: Current through 6Ω with 12V?
In series, current is:
quiz.explanation: One path = same current at every point.

quiz.question: House lights are parallel so:
options: One can be off while others stay on
quiz.explanation: Parallel = independent branches.

quiz.question: Resistance of 10Ω and 10Ω in series:
quiz.explanation: Series resistances add: 10 + 10 = 20Ω.

quiz.question: If voltage doubles and resistance stays the same, current:
quiz.explanation: V = IR. Double V with same R means I must double.

lessons.title: Magnetism
lessons.content: Magnets have north and south poles. Like poles repel, opposite poles attract. A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where forces act — field lines go from north to south. Earth is a giant magnet (compass needles point north). Electromagnets: wire coil around iron core with current — magnetic field can be turned on/off. Stronger with more current, more coils, or an iron core. Used in motors, doorbells, speakers, MRI machines, and scrapyard cranes.
examples: Compass aligns with Earth's magnetic field, pointing north
Scrapyard electromagnet picks up cars — releasing current drops them
Electric motors use switching electromagnets to spin a shaft

keyTerms.magnetic field: Region around a magnet where magnetic forces act
keyTerms.electromagnet: A magnet created by electric current through a coil
keyTerms.poles: The ends of a magnet where force is strongest
keyTerms.solenoid: A coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when current flows

quiz.question: Two north poles brought together:
quiz.explanation: Like poles repel.

quiz.question: How to make an electromagnet stronger:
quiz.explanation: More current or coils = stronger magnetic field.

quiz.question: A compass works because:
quiz.explanation: The magnetized needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field.

quiz.question: Advantage of electromagnets over permanent magnets:
options: Can be turned on and off
quiz.explanation: Electromagnets can be switched — permanent magnets are always on.

quiz.question: Magnetic field lines go from:
options: North to south pole outside the magnet
quiz.explanation: Field lines emerge from north and curve around to enter south.

lessons.title: Static and Current Electricity
lessons.content: Static electricity is charge buildup on surfaces. Rubbing a balloon on hair transfers electrons (balloon becomes negative, hair positive — they attract). Lightning is a massive static discharge. Current electricity is continuous charge flow through conductors. Conductors (metals, especially copper) allow electron flow. Insulators (rubber, plastic, glass) resist it. Electrical power = voltage × current (P = VI). Energy = power × time (E = Pt). Measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) for household billing.
examples: Rubbing feet on carpet + touching doorknob = spark (static discharge)
Lightning: massive charge difference → giant spark
Copper wires conduct well; rubber coating insulates for safety

keyTerms.electrical power: Rate of energy transfer: P = VI, measured in Watts

quiz.question: When rubbing a balloon on hair, what transfers?
quiz.explanation: Electrons transfer between materials, creating static charge.

quiz.question: Best electrical conductor:
quiz.explanation: Copper is an excellent conductor.

quiz.question: Lightning is:
quiz.explanation: Lightning is a massive static discharge between charged clouds and ground.

quiz.question: Power of a 230V, 10A kettle:
Energy used by a 2 kW heater in 3 hours:
quiz.explanation: E = P × t = 2 × 3 = 6 kWh.

lessons.title: The Motor Effect and Electromagnetic Induction
lessons.content: When a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force — this is the motor effect. The direction of force depends on the current direction and field direction (Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: thumb = force, first finger = field, second finger = current). Electric motors use this: current in a coil within a magnetic field causes rotation. The reverse process is electromagnetic induction: moving a wire through a magnetic field (or changing the field around a coil) induces a voltage. This is how generators work — mechanical energy converted to electrical energy. Transformers use induction to change voltage levels for efficient power transmission.
examples: Electric motor: current in coil + magnets → coil spins → powers washing machines, fans, electric cars
Generator: spinning a coil in a magnetic field induces voltage → power stations use this
Transformer: step-up transformers increase voltage for long-distance power lines; step-down transformers reduce it for homes (230V)

keyTerms.motor effect: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
keyTerms.electromagnetic induction: Generating voltage by moving a conductor through a magnetic field
keyTerms.generator: A device converting mechanical energy to electrical energy using induction
keyTerms.transformer: A device that changes voltage levels using electromagnetic induction

lessons.title: Nuclear Physics
lessons.content: Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons orbiting. Radioactive atoms have unstable nuclei that decay, emitting radiation. Three types: alpha (α) — 2 protons + 2 neutrons, stopped by paper, highly ionizing; beta (β) — a fast electron from the nucleus, stopped by aluminium; gamma (γ) — electromagnetic radiation, only reduced by thick lead or concrete. Half-life is the time for half of radioactive atoms to decay. Nuclear fission splits heavy atoms (uranium) releasing enormous energy — used in power stations and atomic bombs. Nuclear fusion joins light atoms (hydrogen → helium) releasing even more energy — powers the Sun.
examples: Carbon-14 dating: half-life of 5,730 years — used to date ancient objects up to ~50,000 years
Nuclear power: controlled fission of uranium-235 heats water → steam → turbine → generator → electricity
The Sun: hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium at 15 million °C, releasing energy that reaches Earth as light and heat

keyTerms.radioactivity: The spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable atomic nuclei
keyTerms.half-life: The time for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay
keyTerms.fission: Splitting a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei, releasing energy
keyTerms.fusion: Joining light nuclei together to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy

quiz.question: Alpha radiation is stopped by:
quiz.explanation: Alpha particles are large and stopped by just a sheet of paper or skin.

quiz.question: Half-life means:
options: Half the size of an atom
Time for half the radioactive atoms to decay
The life of half an atom
quiz.explanation: After one half-life, 50% of the original radioactive atoms remain.

quiz.question: The Sun produces energy by:
quiz.explanation: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium — fusion releases enormous energy.

quiz.question: Nuclear power stations use:
quiz.explanation: Power stations split uranium atoms in controlled fission reactions.

quiz.question: Which radiation is most penetrating?
quiz.explanation: Gamma rays are EM radiation — they pass through most materials, only stopped by thick lead or concrete.
